newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. puts off immediate action on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. puts off immediate action on Zaire.

text.p: With food shortages in eastern Zaire already acute, the United Nations Security Council on Saturday called on U.N. members to lay the groundwork for a multinational force to help feed the hungry.
But the resolution did not authorise an immediate force and it seemed there would be no respite soon for the starving.
In Goma, the biggest east Zaire city captured by rebels in a growing insurrection against President Mobutu Sese Seko, Red Cross officials warned of impending catastrophe.

U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who has warned of "genocide by starvation" in eastern Zaire, was asked by the Security Council to draw up a "concept of operations and framework for a humanitarian task force".

This would deliver aid to the more than one million refugees from ethnic violence in Rwanda and Burundi and plan for their voluntary repatriation. He is to report to the council by a November 20 deadline.

Many council members had hoped to adopt a resolution immediately authorising a multinational force. But this proved impossible after the United States said it was still studying whether it could participate and if so whether with logistics, financial assistance or other contributions.
Boutros-Ghali had pressed for swift action. He said the refugees, scattered by recent fighting in eastern Zaire, lacked food, water and shelter.
The interim resolution asked the states involved to report back as soon as possible to enable the council to give final approval.
Fighting in eastern Zaire has spread death, fear and misery across a vast stretch of territory in the biggest country in Central Africa.
Hundreds of thousands of Zaireans are also on the move and food is increasingly scarce.
In Goma, rioting Zaireans seized the last food from a U.N. warehouse on Friday.
Tabo Dufina, a local official of the International Federation of the Red Cross (IFRC) told Reuters on Saturday: "There will be no distribution of food today because there is no food to distribute.

"It is a disaster, it is a catastrophe. There is no food or other items in any of the warehouses at all. There is no food coming in from Rwanda from humanitarian groups but there is a little bit of local commerce coming across."
Goma was captured by the rebels a week ago after fierce battles which killed about 500 people, according to local IFRC estimates.
Zaire hardened its tone on Friday, stating categorically it would no longer allow the Rwandan and Burundian refugees on its soil.
"No new refugee camps can be built anywhere in Zaire," Information Minister Boguo Makeli declared on state television, reading from decisions of a cabinet meeting.

Most of the existing camps for Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire from Rwanda and Burundi in 1994 after Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis have been abandoned in three weeks of battles between rebels and the army in eastern Zaire.
U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien arrived in Kinshasa on Friday night from Rwanda to pursue talks on the proposed multinational force to help refugees dying in thousands in the bush.
All relief aid for displaced Zaireans must be landed in the capital Kinshasa, Boguo said in the declaration made shortly after Chretien arrived from Rwanda.
The U.N. World Food Programme warned the world of mass death in the next three weeks without humanitarian aid corridors.
"People are already starving to death and we estimate that by the end of the month over 80,000 children under three will die," Catherine Bertini, WFP's executive director told Reuters.
Bernard Pecoul, head of Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders), estimated in Paris more than 13,600 refugees died in the last three weeks, not including victims of fighting.

Hutu refugees, desperate Zaireans and demoralised soldiers in Zaire's ragged army are roaming the east region. Some have staggered on swollen legs into Kisangani, up to 500 km (300 miles) from the war zone.
